title: The Mentorship Classroom: Designing Assignments that Help Students Show Their Work
author: Shewmaker, Jennifer et al.
source: Leadership at the Edge of Change (jenshew.substack.com), September 14, 2026
summary: Written as the conclusion to a 'Beyond the Ban' series on AI and academic integrity, this piece argues that the right response to generative AI in classrooms isn't better detection but a redesign of assessment itself around mentorship. Co-authored by a K-12 teacher and a higher-ed faculty member, it proposes a 'Process + Product + Presentation' framework: capturing evidence of a student's thinking trail (notes, drafts, AI documentation), still assessing the finished product, and adding a presentation component where students must explain, defend, or apply what they made. The authors argue that assessing only the final product has always been an imperfect way to see learning, and that AI has simply made the gap unbearable, since a model can generate a polished product without any of the thinking a teacher actually wants to see. Concrete K-12 and higher-ed examples — slowing down the essay-writing process, using a custom AI tutor bot to scaffold productive struggle in a STEM course — ground the framework in practice rather than theory. The piece closes by reframing the AI cheating question itself: not 'did a student cheat' but 'does the student own the learning,' which shifts the teacher's role from AI detective to mentor present throughout the process.
points: Reframes the AI-cheating problem: instead of asking 'did they cheat,' design assessments that make the thinking process itself visible (notes, drafts, revisions, AI documentation).
Offers a concrete three-part framework — Process + Product + Presentation — that can be layered onto existing assignments rather than replacing them.
Documents a real STEM example: a custom AI chatbot ('Gene Genius') built to scaffold productive struggle through open-ended questions rather than giving answers.
Explicitly warns that 'showing your work' can curdle into surveillance if the purpose is proving innocence rather than fostering a genuine mentoring relationship.
quotes: In the age of generative AI, it's tempting to believe the answer lies in better detection, tighter restrictions, or increasingly complex rules. However, we believe there's a better answer. Instead of focusing on becoming better detectives, what if we focused on becoming better mentors?
What we're learning is that it's more helpful to examine the trail of thinking, including the questions asked, the revisions made, and the reflections that led to the final product.

Of course, asking students to show their work can become surveillance if its primary purpose is proving innocence. In a mentoring classroom, what we're hoping to create is an environment where evidence of the learning process becomes the basis for conversations that foster reflection and growth.

AI can generate a beautifully polished product, but education has never ultimately been about the final product. It has always been about forming people who can question, wrestle with ideas, and create something that reflects their growing understanding.
AI has led us to ask who authored the work. A mentorship classroom asks something more: Does the student own the learning?
